paras: The threatened lynching of Frank Ray and Maxwell Smith took place near Sherman, Texas, in the spring of 1881, when the two men were arrested on charges of attempting outrages on little girls and local citizens grew so excited that the prisoners had to be removed to keep them from being lynched. No attack followed, and both men were later dealt with in the Sherman courts, Smith with a $25 fine and Ray with a five-year prison term. None of the reports gives the race of the accused men or of the girls.

A brief in the Memphis Daily Appeal of April 12, 1881, said only that Ray and Smith had been arrested "recently" near Sherman on charges of attempting to commit outrages on little girls. According to the same item, "the citizens were so excited over the affair" that the prisoners had to be removed to prevent a lynching. The brief did not say who removed them, where they were taken, or how many people took part in the excitement.

In a Sherman dispatch dated May 3, the Dallas Herald reported that Maxwell Smith, "a young man who had been reading Fowler," had been judged guilty in district court of an aggravated assault on an eight-year-old girl and fined twenty-five dollars. The girl's grandfather, the dispatch added, settled the fine and costs. A week later a second Sherman dispatch reported that Frank Ray, "a sixteen-year-old boy," had pleaded guilty to "a villainous crime" and was assessed five years in the penitentiary, though it did not name the offense.

The threat of lynching appeared only in the Memphis Appeal's "News from Our Neighbors" column, a single sentence among regional items on fires, accidents and crimes, with no comment. The Texas papers that followed the case reported the prosecutions in routine court notes and did not mention the threatened lynching. The Weekly Democratic Statesman took a harsher line on Smith, describing him as having begged for mercy when the child's parents discovered him and treating the $25 fine as a light outcome. The Statesman suggested that he would probably leave Sherman and that the press should keep his name before the public.
The papers gave different ages for the girl in Smith's case: eight in the Sherman court dispatch and seven in the Statesman's digest.

bases: The only report of crowd action says Sherman citizens were so excited that the two prisoners had to be removed to keep them from being lynched, a threatened lynching that did not occur (A1).

No one was killed: the prisoners were removed before any attack and were later tried, Smith fined and Ray sentenced to prison (A1, A2, A3). The threat came from excited 'citizens' of unstated number over an accusation of crime (A1).
Only the Memphis brief reports the lynching threat (A1); the Sherman court reports corroborate the charges and prosecutions but say nothing of a mob (A2, A3, A4).

accounts.gist: Ray and Smith were arrested near Sherman for attempted outrages on little girls, and citizens were so excited the prisoners had to be removed to keep them from being lynched.

accounts.label: Sherman court dispatches
accounts.gist: Smith was found guilty of aggravated assault on an eight-year-old girl and fined $25; Ray, sixteen, pleaded guilty to an unnamed 'villainous crime' and got five years.

accounts.label: Texas editorial note
accounts.gist: Smith attempted to violate a seven-year-old, begged mercy when discovered, and got off with a $25 fine that the paper treated as too light.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal ran the threat as one line in a column of regional briefs, between a railroad accident and a Hot Springs licensing dispute, without comment.
The Statesman made no mention of the threatened lynching but called Smith's sentence a 'milk and water' outcome and urged the press to keep his name before the public.
